fields.title: The Secret of Guidance
fields.description: The Secret of Guidance by Frederick Brotherton Meyer is a timeless guide to discerning God’s will and finding lasting purpose. With heartfelt wisdom and practical advice, Meyer offers clarity in tough decisions, comfort in uncertainty, and a deeper connection to faith. This inspiring book explores strengthening the inner self and aligning with divine intentions for a fulfilling life. Perfect for those seeking spiritual growth and guidance. Contents: The Secret of Guidance—Where Am I Wrong?—The Secret of Christ’s indwelling—Fact! Faith! Feeling—Burdens, and What to Do with Them—How to Bear Sorrow—In the Secret of His Presence—The Fullness of the Spirit.

fields.title: The Secret of Guidance
fields.body_html:
Many children of God worry about guidance. I will offer some tips on knowing how our Father wants us to walk and the work He wants us to do. Our power and peace depend on knowing where God wants us to be and being there. We cannot exaggerate their importance.

The manna only falls where the cloudy pillar broods. But, you can certainly find it on the sands that glowed under the heavenly fire's flashing light a few hours ago. They are now shadowed by the fleecy cloud canopy. If we are where our heavenly Father wants us to be, we are sure He will provide food, clothing, and everything else. When He sends His servants to Cherith, He will make even the ravens bring them food.

How much of our Christian work has failed? It is because we have insisted on starting it ourselves. We should have sought to know what God was doing and where He wanted us! We dream bright dreams of success. We try to command it. We call to our aid all kinds of quick fixes, questionable or otherwise. At last we turn back, disheartened and ashamed. We are like children, torn and scratched by thorns, and soiled by the quagmire. None of this would have come about if only we had been, from the first, under God’s perfect guidance. He might test us, but He would not allow us to fail.

The child of God, wanting to know his Father's will, turns to the sacred Book. It restores his faith. It shows how, in all ages, God has guided those who dared to trust Him. But, they must have been as perplexed as we are now. We know how Abraham left his kin and country. With no guide but God, he crossed the trackless desert to a land unknown to him. We know how, for forty years, the Israelites were led through the red sandstone and sand of the Sinai Peninsula.

We know how, in entering the Promised Land, Joshua faced unknown lands and great, warlike nations. He looked to the Captain of the Lord's hosts, who leads to victory. We know that, in the early church, the apostles solved tough problems. They laid down principles to guide the church until the end of time. This was because the Holy Spirit revealed to them what to do and say. The promises for guidance are unmistakable. Psalm 32:8: "I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you." This is God's promise to those whose sins are forgiven. They are more eager to see a hint of His will than horses are to feel the bit.

Proverbs 3:6: “In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.” This is a sure word on which we may rest. But, we must trust with all our heart and not lean on our own understanding. Isaiah 58:11: "And the LORD will guide you continually and satisfy your desire in scorched places and make your bones strong." If He did not always guide us, we could not think He could guide us at all. Life's greatest events hinge on tiny points. Like the huge rocking stones in western England. A pebble may alter the flow of a stream. The growth of a grain of mustard seed may determine the rainfall of a continent. We are bidden to seek guidance for all of life and its essentials.

John 8:12: Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world.” Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." This refers to the wilderness wanderings. The Master promises to be, to all faithful souls in their pilgrimage to the City of God, what the cloudy pillar was to the Israelites on their march to the Promised Land. These are but samples. The Bible's treasure is full of insights. They shine like stars, guiding a lost traveler at sea. The prophet sums up the heritage of the Lord's servants. He says of the Holy City, "All your children shall be taught by the LORD, and great shall be the peace of your children." (Isaiah 54:13).

Some may think, with their timid hearts, that everyone in the Bible was helped. But, they are left without help. They seem to have faced life's mysteries. They long to know what to do. But, no angel has come to tell them. No iron gate has opened in the prison of circumstances.

Some lay the blame on their own stupidity. Their minds are blunt and dull. They cannot catch God’s meaning, which would be clear to others.

Their fear of making mistakes prevents them from understanding what is right. “Who is blind but my servant, or deaf as my messenger whom I send? Who is blind as my dedicated one, or blind as the servant of the LORD?” (Isaiah 42:19). Yet, how do we treat our children? One child is so bright that a hint shows the way. Another, born dull, cannot grasp your meaning quickly. Do you only let the clever one know what you want? Will you not take the other upon your knee and make clear to him the confusing directions?

Does not the tiny child's distress, to know he may obey, weave a stronger bond than that which binds you to the rest? Oh, weary, perplexed, and stupid children! Believe in God's great love. Trust it. He will meet your needs and come down to your ignorance. "He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young.” (Isaiah 40:11). We must attend to certain practical directions to be led into the mind of the Lord.

Our Motives Must Be Pure “Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness” (Luke 11:34). You have been much in darkness lately, and this passage will point up the reason. Your eye has been distracted from its primary focus. A spiritual squint has blurred your vision.

It has hindered you from seeing signs of God's will, which would have been as clear as noon. We must be very careful in judging our motives. We should search them, as the Commons' detectives search each stranger who enters. By God's grace, we are free from gross sin. But, we are still prone to the subtle workings of the self in our holiest, loveliest hours. It poisons our motives.

It breathes decay on our fairest fruit-bearing. It whispers seductive flatteries into our pleased ears. It turns the spirit from its holy purpose. The masses of iron on ocean steamers deflect the compass needle from the pole.

If there is any thought of personal gain, we can't know God's purpose for us. The door must remain firmly shut against all these if we are to hear the still small voice. We must exclude all cross-lights. Only then could we see the Urim and Thummim stones. They would brighten with God's "Yes" or darken with His "No." Ask the Holy Spirit for a single eye. Let it inspire in you one aim alone: that which drove our Lord. It let Him cry to the Father, "For we never came with flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness." Nor did we seek glory from people, whether from you or others. Though we could have made demands as apostles of Christ." (1 Thessalonians 2:5-6) Then, "If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light" (Luke 11:36). We must surrender our will.

“I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.” (John 5:30). This was the secret that Jesus practiced and taught.

He repeatedly insisted that a surrendered will was the key to perfect knowledge. “If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority.” (John 7:17).

An extinguished will differs from a surrendered one. God does not demand that we crush our wills, like a fakir’s unused arms. He only asks that we should say “Yes” to Him. We ought to be as flexible toward Him as the willow branch is to the practised hand.

Many times, as the steamer neared the bank, I watched the little lad. He took his place beneath the poop, eyes and ears fixed on the captain. He waited to shout each word to the grimy engineers below. I often longed for my will to, as the Lord's, obey. I wanted my words to match God's, so all my lower nature might obey.

It is for the lack of this subordination that we so often miss the guidance we seek. There is a secret controversy between our will and God’s. And we will never be right till we have let Him take, break, and make. Oh! Do seek for that. If you cannot give, let Him take. If you are not willing, confess that you are willing to become willing. Hand yourself over to Him to work in you, to will and to do His own good pleasure. We must be like plastic clay. We should be ready to take any shape that the great Potter may choose. Only then can we detect His guidance.

We must Seek Information for Our Mind. This is undoubtedly the next step. God has given us these wonderful faculties of brainpower, and He will not ignore them.

In grace, He does not cancel His marvellous gifts. But, He uses them to communicate His purposes and thoughts. We must, then, feed our minds with facts and reliable information. We should learn from human experience and, above all, the Word of God. It is admirable how full the Bible is of biography and history. Hardly any crisis in our lives can match those wondrous pages. There is no book like the Bible for casting a light on the dark landing of human life.

We don’t need to run to our friends for advice. But, we should gather reliable information. It can feed and strengthen our holy thoughts and purpose. We must decide, as God shall teach us. His voice may come through sanctified common sense, using what we have learned. At times, God may ask us to act against our reason. These times are very rare. Our duty will be so clear that there can be no mistake. But, for the most part, God will speak in the results of a careful weighing of the pros and cons.

An angel rescued Peter from prison. But, after a street or two, the angel left him to consider the matter. That is the way God treats us too. He will dictate a miraculous course by miraculous methods. But when the ordinary light of reason is adequate to the task, He will leave us to act as occasion may serve.

We Must Be Much in Prayer for Guidance The Psalms have many pleas for clear direction: "Teach me your way, O Lord, and lead me on a level path because of my enemies."” (Psalm 27:11). It is the law of our Father’s house that His children must ask for what they want.

"If any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives to all without reproach. And God will give it to him." In a time of change and crisis, we must pray. We should be on our knees, but also in a sweet, inward prayer. It is a spirit that constantly asks God to show His will. We seek to have His will impressed upon our spirit, like heavenly bodies on prepared paper.

The trustful believer, wrapped in prayer, may tread the deck of the ocean steamer night after night. He who points the stars will not fail to guide a soul whose only aim is to do His will.

A good prayer is to ask God to shut doors, close the way, and halt all ventures against His will at their start. From the outset, put the matter in God's hands. He will shatter any project that is not according to His holy will.

We must wait for God's plan to unfold. We should trust His impressions and His word, which His providence supports. We should also wait in silence until these three converge into one point.

Sometimes it looks as if we are bound to act. Everyone says we must act. Things are so desperate that we must. The Egyptians are behind us. Inaccessible cliffs are on our sides. The sea is in front. It is not easy at such times to stand still and see the salvation of God, but we must. Saul made the biggest mistake of his life. He compelled himself and offered a sacrifice, thinking Samuel was late in coming. God may delay to come in the guise of His providence.

There was delay before Sennacherib’s host lay like withered leaves around the Holy City. There was a delay before Jesus walked on the sea at dawn or hastened to raise Lazarus. There was a delay before the angel sped to Peter's side on the night before his expected martyrdom. God waits long enough to test patience of faith, but not a moment behind the extreme hour of need. “For still the vision awaits its appointed time; it hastens to the end—it will not lie. If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay. (Habakkuk 2:3).

It is remarkable how God guides us by circumstances. At one moment, the way may seem blocked. Then, a trivial incident occurs. It may not seem much to others. But, to the keen eye of faith, it speaks volumes. Sometimes these signs are repeated in different ways in answer to prayer. They are not random results of chance, but the opening up of circumstances in the direction in which we should walk. And they begin to multiply as we advance toward our goal, just as lights do as we near a populous town when darting through the land by night express.

Sometimes, men sigh for an angel to show them the way. That means the time has not yet come for them to move. If you do not know what you ought to do, stand still until you do. When it's time for action, circumstances will sparkle like glow worms along your path. You will be so sure you are right, when God’s three witnesses agree, that you could not be more sure though an angel beckoned you on.

Our daily life is a reliable sign of God's will. This is true when it aligns with the Spirit's promptings and the Word of God. So long as they are stationary, wait. When you must act, they will open.

A way will be made through oceans, rivers, wastes, and rocks. We often make a great mistake. We think that God is not guiding us, because we cannot see far ahead. But this is not His method. He only undertakes that the steps of a good man should be ordered by the Lord. Not next year, but tomorrow. Not the next mile, but the next yard. Not the whole pattern, but the next stitch in the canvas. If you expect more than this, you will be disappointed and get back into the dark. But, this will secure for you leading in the right way. You will acknowledge this when you review it from the hilltops of glory.

We cannot ponder too deeply the lessons of the cloud. It is given in the exquisite picture-lesson on guidance (Numbers 9:15–23).

" On the day that the tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the tent of the testimony. And at evening it was over the tabernacle like the appearance of fire until morning. So it was always: the cloud covered it by day and the appearance of fire by night. And whenever the cloud lifted from over the tent, after that the people of Israel set out, and in the place where the cloud settled down, there the people of Israel camped. At the command of the LORD the people of Israel set out, and at the command of the LORD they camped. As long as the cloud rested over the tabernacle, they remained in camp. Even when the cloud continued over the tabernacle many days, the people of Israel kept the charge of the LORD and did not set out ." (Numbers 9:15-19) “ Sometimes the cloud was a few days over the tabernacle, and according to the command of the LORD they remained in camp; then according to the command of the LORD they set out. And sometimes the cloud remained from evening until morning. And when the cloud lifted in the morning, they set out, or if it continued for a day and a night, when the cloud lifted, they set out. Whether it was two days, or a month, or a longer time that the cloud continued over the tabernacle abiding there, the people of Israel remained in camp and did not set out, but when it lifted, they set out. At the command of the LORD, they camped, and at the command of the LORD, they set out. “They kept the charge of the LORD, at the command of the LORD by Moses.”(Numbers 9:20-23) Let us look high enough for guidance. Let us encourage our souls to wait only upon God until He gives it. Let us cultivate that meekness that He will guide in judgment. Let us seek to understand with great urgency, so we may incline ourselves to see the least sign of His will. Let us stand with girded loins and lighted lamps, prompting us to obey. Blessed are those servants. The right way will lead them to the golden city of the saints. I have waited and prayed for months. I am sure of my heavenly Father's guidance. I urge any troubled readers to wait for the Lord. He will show His will in time.

Let us seek to understand with great urgency, so we may incline ourselves to see the least sign of His will. Let us stand with girded loins and lighted lamps, prompting us to obey. Blessed are those servants. The right way will lead them to the golden city of the saints. I have waited and prayed for months. I am sure of my heavenly Father's guidance. I urge any troubled readers to wait for the Lord. He will show His will in time.

fields.title: Where Am I Wrong?
fields.body_html:
This is your eager question, O Christian soul, and your bitter complaint. You see a light, a joy, a power in people you know. You envy it, which oppresses you. But, you should thank God for it. It's good to be dissatisfied with our low aspirations. It can lead us to seek a sweeter, nobler, and more triumphant life. The restless sleeper is near awakening. The morning light now shines around the bed, where he has slept too long. For, anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” (Ephesians 5:14).

We must, yet, remember that personalities differ. Some seem born in the dark, and carry a tendency to sadness with them through life. Their nature is set to a minor key and responds with ease to depression.

They always look on the dark side of things and in the bluest of skies discover the cloud no bigger than a man’s hand. Theirs is a dark path. Tiny sunbeams struggle to break through the thick, leafy canopy above. You may have such a temperament. If so, don't expect the same joy that others feel. And, don't complain if you don't feel it.

Your Savior’s hands made this burden for you. You must carry it for Him. Do not complain, show it to others, or let it master your spirit. Bear it silently, and glorify God through it all. But it may be impossible to win the joy of others. At least, there may be rest, victory, and peace. They are heaven's best gifts to man.

We must also remember that emotion is no true test of our spiritual state. A right heart often shows in a glad heart. So, good health usually shows in high spirits. But it is not always so. In other words, the absence of joy does not always prove that the heart is wrong. It may do so, but it will not always happen. The wilderness may have overtaxed Elijah's nervous system. After the long strain of Carmel and his flight, he lay on the sand and asked to die. God met that request, not with a rebuke, but with food and sleep.

The Lord has darkened your land. He wants to test if you love Him for Himself or for His gifts.

Perhaps, life has reached a Gethsemane. A Father's hand places a bitter cup to our lips, though only a Judas appears. We feel anguish in our struggle to renounce our will. It is only possible to lie upon the ground, with strong crying and tears, which the night wind bears to God. Under such circumstances as these, exuberant joy is out of place.

Sombre colours become the tried and suffering soul.

High spirits would be as unbecoming here as cheerfulness in the home shadowed by death. At such times, we should manifest patience, courage, and faith as the suitable graces. Yet, with all that, many of us are at fault. We are missing a blessedness that would make us radiant with the light of paradise. This loss is due to some flaw in our character. We should find and fix it.

You Do Not Distinguish Between Your Standing and Your Experience Our experiences are as fickle as April weather. Now sunshine, now cloud. Lights and shadows chase each other over miles of wild fields or a foamy sea. But our standing in Jesus changes not. It is like Himself—the same yesterday, today, and forever. It did not come from us. It came from His everlasting love. It, foreseeing all we would be, loved us despite it all. We have not purchased it, but His precious blood. It pleads for us with great strength and effectiveness when our faith is weak. It is not maintained by us, but by the Holy Spirit.

If we have fled to Jesus for salvation, we are one with Him forever. We have sheltered under Him, relying on and trusting Him, though with some doubts. We were one with Him in the grave; one with Him on Easter morning; one with Him when He sat down at God’s right hand. We are one with Him now. He stands in the light of His Father's smile. It's like a swimmer's limbs are one with his head. The sun's warm glory encircles the head alone. The waves hide the arms and legs. No doubt or depression can affect our acceptance with God through the blood of Jesus. That is an eternal fact.

You may not realize this. But, have your moods affected your standing in Jesus? A wealthy heiress's fortune could change with her spending money. Our standing in Jesus is our invested capital. Our emotions, at best, are like our spending money. It is always passing through our pocket or purse, never the same. Consider how you feel. Build on the rock of what Jesus is, has done, is doing, and will do for you, forever.

You Live Too Much in Your Feelings, Too Little in Your Will. We have no direct control over our feelings, but we have over our will. Our wills are ours, to make them God’s. God does not hold us responsible for what we feel, but for what we will. In His sight, we are not what we feel, but what we will. Let us not live in the summerhouse of emotion. Instead, let us live in the stronghold of the will, devoted to God's will.

At the Lord's Table, holy emotion often fills the soul. The tides rise high. Joy's powerful waves knock loudly against the floodgates. Every part of nature joins in a choral hymn of praise. But the next day comes. Life must be faced in the grimy counting house, the dingy shop, the noisy factory, and the godless workroom. The soul, comparing yesterday's joy with today's struggle, doubts its devotion to the Lord.

But, at such a time, how fair it is to remark that the will has not altered its position by a hair's breadth. And to look up and say: "My God, the spring tide of emotion has passed away like a summer brook. But in my heart, you know I am devoted and loyal.

I long to be only for You, as in that blessed moment at Your feet." This is an offering with which God is well pleased. And thus we may live a calm and peaceful life.

You Have Disobeyed Some Clear Command. A soul sometimes comes to its spiritual adviser, saying: "I have no joy, and little for years." “Did you once have it?”

“Yes, for some time after my conversion to God.”

"Are you aware that you disobeyed a specific command?

"It came into your life, but you shrank from it."

The face fell. Tears filled the eyes. The answer came, with difficulty: "Yes, years ago, I thought God required something of me. But I felt I could not do what He wished."

I was uneasy for some time about it, but after a while it seemed to fade from my mind, and now it does rarely trouble me.” "Ah, soul, that's where you went wrong. You will never get right until you go back through the weary years to where you dropped the thread of obedience. You must perform that one thing God demanded of you long ago. It is why you left the narrow path of blind obedience. Is this not the cause of depression for thousands of Christians? They are God’s children, but they are disobedient children.

The Bible rings with one long demand for obedience. The key phrase of the book of Deuteronomy is, “Observe and Do.”

The burden of Christ’s farewell discourse is, “If you love me, you will keep my commandments.” We must not question or reply, or excuse ourselves. We must not pick and choose our way. We must not take some commands and reject others. We must not believe that obedience elsewhere will make up for disobedience in one area. God gives one command at a time, borne in upon us, not in one way only, but in many; by this He tests us. If we obey in this, He will flood our souls with blessings and lead us forward into new paths and pastures. But if we refuse, we will remain stagnant and waterlogged. We will make no progress in our Christian experience and lack both power and joy.

You Are Permitting Some Known Evil When water stands, the particles of silt betray themselves as they fall one by one to the bottom. So if you are quiet, you may become aware of the presence in your soul of permitted evil. Dare to consider it. Do not avoid the sight like a bankrupt man avoids his ledgers, or a sick man avoids a stethoscope. Consider, in silence, any evil the Spirit of God finds in your soul. It may have lurked in the closets and cloisters of your being for years, suspected but unjudged. But whatever it is, and its history, it brings your daily sorrow.

Does your will you refuse to give up a practice or habit that is foreign to the will of God? Do you permit some secret sin to have its unhindered way in the house of your life? Do your affections roam unrestrained after forbidden objects? Do you cherish any resentment or hatred toward someone with whom you refuse to reconcile? Is there an injustice you won't forgive? A debt you won't pay? A wrong you won't confess?

Are you allowing in yourself something you would condemn in others? You justify it for certain reasons to silence your conscience.

Sometimes, the hindrance of bliss lies not in sins but in burdens that weigh on the soul. Sin is that which is always and everywhere wrong. A weight is anything that hinders the Christian life, but is not a sin. Thus, a thing may be a weight to one that is not so to another. Each must reach complete conviction in his own mind. If the soul knows that anything hinders its life, it must be cast aside. This is true, regardless of the harmlessness or innocent permission of that thing. You must discard it, like the garments of athletes who compete for a prize in wrestling or racing.

You Look Too Much Inward on Self, Instead of Outward on the Lord Jesus The healthiest people don't think about their health. The weak cause disease by overthinking. If you begin to count your heartbeats, you will disturb the rhythmic action of the heart. If you repeatedly imagine a pain anywhere, you will produce it. Some true children of God induce their own darkness by morbid self-scrutiny. They always go back on themselves. They analyze their motives. They rethink past acts of devotion. They compare themselves to themselves. In one form or another, the self is the pivot of their life, even if it is a religious life. What but darkness can result from such a course? At times in our lives, we must look within and check ourselves to avoid others judging us.

But this is only done so that we may turn with the fuller purpose of heart to the Lord. Once you complete it, you don’t need to repeat it.

“Leaving the things behind” is the only safe motto. The question is not if we did our best, but if we did as well as we could at the time. We must not waste our lives cleaning our windows, or in worrying if they are clean. We must enjoy God's blessed light. That light will soon show us what must be cleansed.

It will let us cleanse it with perfect accuracy. Our Lord Jesus is a perfect reservoir of everything the soul of man requires for a blessed and holy life.

To be healthy in soul, we must make much of Him. We must abide in Him, draw from Him, and receive each moment from His fullness. To care for self-more than for Him is like this: Spending much time on the body's senses, but never using them to sense the world outside.

Look unto Jesus. “Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 37:4). “For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him.” (Psalm 62:5).

You Spend Too Little Time in Communion with God through His Word Long prayers are not necessary. But it is essential to be alone with God. Wait at His door, hear His voice, and linger in Scripture for the Lord's coming at dawn or in the cool of the day. No meetings, no Christian friends, and no activity can replace the neglect of the still hour.

When you feel least inclined for it, there is most need to go into your closet with the door shut. Do for duty’s sake what you cannot do as a pleasure, and you will find it becomes delightful.

You can thrive without food. But you cannot find joy or strength in a Christian life without fellowship with God. When you cannot pray for yourself, begin to pray for others. When your desires fade, take the Bible. Turn each text into a petition. Or, recall your mercies. Then, translate each into praise.

When the Bible bores you, check your appetite. Have you spoiled it with sweets? If so, renounce them. The Word is the wire along which God's voice will come to you. But your heart must be still and your mind focused. “Let me hear what God the Lord will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his saints; but let them not turn back to folly.” (Psalm 85:8). More Christians than we can count are suffering from a lack of prayer and Bible study. No one desires a revival more than that of systematic private Bible study. No short and easy method of godliness can dispense with this.

You have never fully surrendered yourself to the authority of the Lord Jesus .

We are His by many ties and rights, but too few of us recognize His lordship. We are willing enough to take Him as Savior but hesitate to make Him King. We forget that God has exalted Him to be Prince, as well as Savior, and the divine order is irreversible.

Those who ignore the Lordship of Jesus cannot build a strong or happy life. Put the sun in its central throne, and all the motions of the planets assume a beautiful order. Put Jesus on the throne of your life, and all things fall into harmony and peace. Seek first the kingdom of God, and all things are yours.

Consecration is the indispensable condition of blessedness. So will light break on your path, such as has not shone there for many days. Yes, "Your sun shall no more go down, nor your moon withdraw. For the Lord will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning shall end.” (Isaiah 60:20).

fields.title: The Secret of Christ’s indwelling
fields.body_html:
It is fitting that the largest church in the greatest Gentile city is dedicated to the apostle Paul. Gentiles owe him a great debt as the Apostle of the Gentiles. We owe, under the Spirit of God, to him. He unveiled two great mysteries that especially touch us as Gentiles. We cannot discuss, now, the first of these, glorious as it is. It sparked a revolution when first preached by the apostle, despite fierce opposition. Until then, Gentiles had to become Jews before they could be Christians.

They had to go through the synagogue to reach the church. But Paul showed that this was not needful. He proved that Gentiles were equal to Jews in their gospel privileges. They were fellow heirs, and members of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel (Ephesians 3:6). “The mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs. They are members of the same body and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.”

The second one deserves more thought. If God's children realized it, they would live divinely. This would silence the enemy and, to some extent, repeat Jesus's life on earth.

The mystery is that the Lord Jesus is willing to dwell within the Gentile heart. Many viewed the expectation for Him to dwell in Abraham's children's hearts as patronizing. But, it was unbelievable to think He could find a home in a Gentile's heart.

This mistake, however, vanished before the truth. He realized that he was unfit to be called an apostle because he had persecuted God's church. God revealed through him, "To them, God chose to reveal among the Gentiles the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory."(Colossians 1:27).

“Master, where do you dwell?” they asked. In reply, Jesus led them from the crowded Jordan bank to a "tent of woven willows," where He stayed for a short time. But if we ask Him now, He will not point to the high, lofty dome of heaven or the splendid stone or marble structure. He will point to the happy spirit that loves, trusts, and obeys Him. “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me." Revelations 3:20. "Jesus answered him, 'If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.” John 14:23. He promised to be within each believer, like a tenant in a house, sap in a branch, and lifeblood in a body.

The Mystery Christ is in the believer. He indwells in the heart by faith. It is like the sun indwelling the lowly flowers that open their petals to its rays. Not because we are good, or because we are making a sincere effort to consecrate ourselves. Not because we keep Him by the tenacity of our love.

But because we believe, and in believing have thrown open all the doors and windows of nature. And He has come in. He entered without making a sound, and we failed to detect His entrance. There was no footfall along the passage.

The golden bells at the bottom of His priestly robe did not betray Him. He arrived at dawn, like nature waking from her winter's sleep and putting on her Creator's robes. But this is the way of Christ. He neither strives nor cries, nor causes His voice to be heard. His tread is so light that it does not break bruised reeds. His breath is so soft that it can re- illuminate dying sparks. So, do not be surprised if you cannot tell the day or the hour when the Son of Man comes to dwell within you. Only believe that He has come. “Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!” (2 Corinthians 13:5).

It is very wonderful. The heavens, even the heavens of heavens, with all their light and glory, alone seem worthy of Him. But even there He is not more at home than He is with the humble and contrite spirit that simply trusts in Him.

In His early life, He said the Father dwelt in Him so truly that His words and works were not His, but His Father's. He wants to be in us as His Father was in Him. Our lives should be channels for His hidden self to reach men.

It is not generally recognized. That does not disprove it. We fail to recognize many things in ourselves and in nature around us that are still true. But many whose natures are Christ's temple ignore the wonderful Tenant within. There is a reason for this. He dwells so deep. Below the body's life, which is like a tent's curtain; below the soul's, where thought, feeling, and imagination roam like white-stoled priests in a holy place; below the play of light and shade, will and memory, and the ebb and flow of self-consciousness. There, through the Holy Spirit, Christ dwells. The Shekinah once did in the Most Holy Place, hidden from man's view.

We rarely explore these deeper departments of our being. We are content to live the superficial life of sense. We eat, we drink, and we sleep. We give ourselves to enjoy the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. We fulfill the desires of the flesh and the mind. Or we abandon ourselves to the pursuit of knowledge and culture, of science and art.

We make short incursions into the realm of morals, that sense of right and wrong that is part of the makeup of men. But, we know too little of the spirit's deeper, mysterious chamber. So, most believers are unaware of their divine, wonderful Resident. He makes the regenerated spirit His home.

fields.title: Fact! Faith! Feeling!
fields.body_html:
These three words stand for three important factors in character and life. We all must deal with them in some way. But, we must put them in the right order. That is most important. Most people try to put feelings first. It's as successful as trying to build the top story of a house before laying its foundations.

Some seek faith first. They ignore the facts that support it. They resemble a man who, wanting warmth on a frosty night, refuses to approach the bright fire on the hearth. The only possible order that will bring blessing and comfort to the heart is that indicated in our title: 1. God’s facts, laid like a foundation of adamant. 2. Our faith, apprehending and resting on them.

3. Joyous feelings, coming all at once or after the lapse of days and months, as God wills.

Fact The Bible tells us facts that are like stepping stones across a brook. Before you reach the shallows where they lie, you wonder how to get over. But when you step to the water's edge, you see they span the space from bank to bank. When you have reached one, you can step to another, and so get across. It is absurd to consult feelings or seek faith while distant from the Brookside. It is also foolish to go above or below that primitive stone bridge. You must come down to them. Check how fixed they are in the muddy ground.

Observe the villagers' effortless passage. Then, you will trust them. Finally, with relief, step from one to another. Let us recall a few facts that may guide us first to faith, and then to feeling. It is a fact that God loves each of us with the tenderest and most particular love. You may not believe it. The warm summer sun may be shining on your closed curtains. But it is not felt inside. Your failure to appreciate God's love cannot change its existence.

In Jesus, every obstacle to your forgiveness and acceptance is gone. God was the dying Saviour. He was putting away sin. He bore our sins in His own body on the tree. He reconciled the world to Himself. You may not believe this, or feel the joy of it, but that does not alter the fact that it is so. After the North and South signed a peace treaty, the Civil War. Some soldiers were hiding in the woods, struggling to survive on berries. They might have returned home. They either did not know or did not believe the good news. So, they starved long after their families had welcomed their comrades. They lost. But, their doubts did not change the fact. They proclaimed peace and opened the door for their return.

A friend may have paid all my debts in my native town, from which I have fled fearing arrest and disgrace. He may have done it with such speed that he never impaired my credit. There may be all the old love and honour waiting to greet me. He may have told me so. But, if I stay away, my folly can't undo those kind acts. It only adds to my misery.

It is a fact that the moment a person trusts Christ, he is born into God’s family and becomes a child of God. There is no doubt about this. You may not feel good, or earnest, or anxious; you may even be conscious of recent failure. You may feel a deep, dark depression. But, if you have received Christ and placed your trust in Him, you have been born again. “ Who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. ” (John 1:13). You may be a prodigal or inconsistent child, but you are a child.

If you were wise you would take the child’s place at the Father’s table and enjoy His smiles. They await you! But, if you stay out in the cold like the elder brother in the parable, you won't change that your place is ready for you. It will be, when you will. It is a fact that God takes what we give, and as soon as we give it. There is no long interval. When we let go, He receives. We are immediately sealed as His when we place ourselves on His altar. When we consecrate ourselves, He accepts. The divine act is instantaneous. You may not be aware of this, and you may continue giving yourself day after day. If you do, you create needless anxiety. You give what is not yours to give. And, you lose the joy of being the absolute property, chattel, and slave of the blessed Master.

But your mistake cannot change the fact that God took you at your word when you first dedicated yourself to Him. Must our lack of faith have no effect on the faithfulness of God?

In Jesus Christ, we sit in heavenly places. We cannot alter this. We may not believe it. We may not enjoy the nearness to Jesus. But, we have a right to it. It is our place in the divine order. A tiny bit of faith unites us with Jesus. We are as one with Him as the loftiest saints. Where the Head is, there is also the Body.

In Him we died on the cross and so met the righteous demands of the holy law. In Him we lay in the grave, and so passed out of the region ruled by the prince of the power of the air. In Him we rose and ascended far above all might and dominion, principality and power.

Is Satan under Christ’s feet? In God’s purpose, he is under ours also.

Are death and the grave forever behind Christ? So, in God’s purpose, we have passed to the Easter side of them both and are to the windward of the storm. Regarding their sting or terror, they resemble the Egyptians, dead on the seashore. Has the great High Priest passed through the heavens within the veil? In God's purpose, we have passed from the outer court into the Holy Place. There, we offer gifts, sacrifices, supplications, and intercessions for all men.

This may seem unreal and impossible. But, it is true. So is Cinderella's wish to marry a prince. These are the facts of the eternal world, whether you avail yourself of them or not. Some records show that former slaves starved in bondage for refusing to escape.

They also tell of noble men who lived hard lives because they would not claim their rights. It is a fact that there is a share in the gift of Pentecost waiting for each member of Christ. Grace has given each one a gift.

The promise of the Holy Spirit is to as many as the Lord our God will call. You have a share in that infilling, that divine function, that power in service. It transformed the apostles from timid sheep to fierce lions in fight. You may never have put in your claim, but there is no grace that others have that you may not get. All things are yours.

God has made over you the unsearchable riches of Christ. No eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor man's heart conceived, all the grace, love, and power that are yours in Christ. The Divine Deposit Bank stores them for you. It is a pity that you live a beggar's life when you have such wealth and power. But, if you choose to do so, your folly does not change the fact that the fullness of God is yours in Christ. The Word of God has revealed these facts. They will help us cross the brook of troubled emotions to solid ground. Let's stop worrying about our faith or our emotions. Let's trust in them. They are more stable than heaven or earth.

Faith If you want true faith, do not think about it, but look away to the facts we have been speaking. We find no difficulty in trusting our friends, because we open our heart, like south windows, to their love. We recall all their interpositions on our behalf. We remember all they have promised and performed.

Where would we place our troubles about faith if we ceased worrying about it? And instead focused on the object of faith—Jesus Christ our Lord?

"Happy are they who have an observatory in their heart- house. They can often retire beneath the great arch of eternity. There, they can use their telescope to view the mighty constellations. Our need should make us seek and claim the intended blessing to meet it.

fields.title: Burdens, and What to Do with Them
fields.body_html:
Do you keep the Sabbath? Not the literal seventh-day rest, but the inner rest of which that day was the blessed type. The pause in life's bustle was a parable. It mirrored an eternal hush, for all men, for now, not the hereafter. The Sabbath-keeping that awaits God's people is for all faithful souls. The storms that have swept around it leave it unchanged. They may take it when they will and carry it with them.

Through dusky land and a wrangling mart, they toiled. Their secret souls repeated a holy strain. Their feet grew busier. This is a strain borrowed from the eternal chords and harmonies of the life and being of God. The secret of Sabbath-keeping is in the absence of burden bearing. "Thus says the LORD: For your lives, take care. Do not carry a burden on the Sabbath or bring it through Jerusalem's gates." And do not carry a burden out of your houses on the Sabbath or do any work” (Jeremiah 17:21–22).

And in the words that follow, the continual presence of a king is made to hinge on obedience to burdens. Nehemiah was so urgent that he set his servants at the city gates, as they crowned the grey summit of Zion.

" As soon as it began to grow dark at the gates of Jerusalem before the Sabbath, I commanded that the doors should be shut and gave orders that they should not be opened until after the Sabbath. And I stationed some of my servants at the gates, that no load might be brought in on the Sabbath day” (Nehemiah 13:19). And what was true in those bygone days is always true.

True Sabbath keeping is impossible if burdens enter the soul. As well as try to sleep when a party of high-spirited, healthy children is tearing up and down the house and playing hide-and-seek in all the rooms. Care will break the rest of the soul as much as sin does. We will not know the peace that passes all understanding. We must learn to shut the door to the burden-carrying thoughts from the world below. They come up the hill, filling our spirits with their noise and cries.

We do not need to stay to describe the results that burden-bearing brings to the heavy-laden. They are evident in the careworn look, the weary eye, and the heavy step. But, deeper than these, there is no power in prayer. There is no joy in God. There are no green pastures, no waters of rest. As snowflakes in the arctic or sand grains in the tropics will build a rampart before some lowly dwelling, enough to exclude the light, so will worries, each tiny in itself, shut out the light of God from the soul and make midnight where God meant midday.

Burden-bearing sadly dishonours God. As men of the world see the faces of those who claim to be God's children, they may wonder what sort of Father He is. Their faces are dark with the same shadows as those on their own. Whatever a man’s profession is, we cannot help judging him by his children's faces. If we judge God by the views of some of His children, His foes' harshest criticisms are almost true.

The unbeliever may argue: "Either there is no God, or He is powerless, uncaring, or indifferent." "What good will religion be to me?" We are either a libel or a Bible; harbour lights or warning signals; magnetic or repellent. Which we are depends on how we treat our burdens.

Of course, there is a difference between care and pain. We can bear our anxieties. But we must suffer according to God's will. We must not take lightly the sufferings our Father sends. They teach lessons only learned in the school where our Lord learned obedience. The chastened spirit must go softly and withdraw itself to suffer. But accepting the sufferings sent from God is very different from burden- bearing. The Father’s care will be clear. There will be no worries and no fears about the future. To the eye of faith, it gleams like the sunlit sea on the horizon, though dark clouds brood above.

Before we are fully awake in the morning, we feel a hint of depression, as if all is not right. A voice seems to tell a long tale of burdens to be carried and difficulties to be faced as the hours pass.

“Ah!” says the voice, “a miserable day will this be.”

“How so?” we inquire, fearfully. A creditor must be met, a skein untangled, an irritation soothed, and some tempers confronted.

It is no use praying. Better linger where you are, and then drag through the day as you can. You are like a martyr being led to his death.”

We have too often yielded to the suggestion. We have dragged ourselves wearily through the hours, doing our daily tasks. Our hands are engaged and our strength spent by the burdens we have assumed. God is pledged to give strength for all duties that He sets, but not for the burdens that we elect to take on as well.

The one cure for burden-bearing is to cast all burdens on the Lord.

The margin of the Revised Version of Psalm 55:22 thus reads: “Cast your burden on the LORD.” Whatever burden the Lord has given you, give it back to Him. Treat the burden of care as you once did the burden of sin; kneel down and deliberately hand it over to Jesus. Say to Him, “Lord, I entrust You with this, and this, and this. I cannot carry them; they are crushing me, but I definitely commit all of them to You to manage, adjust, and arrange. You have taken my sins. Take my sorrows, and in exchange give me Your peace, and Your rest.”

As George Herbert says, “We must put them all into Christ’s bag.” Won’t our Lord Jesus be at least as true and faithful as the best earthly friend we have ever known? Have there not been, at times, a weariness in us all? We have been too tired or helpless to help ourselves. In those moments, we have anxiously handed our troubles to a strong man. We were sure he would not rest until he had solved them. Surely, He who loved us enough to die for us may be trusted to arrange all the smaller matters of our daily lives!

Of course, we must meet one or two conditions. Then, we can hand our burdens to the Lord Jesus and leave them with Him in perfect confidence.

1. We must have cast our sins on Him before we can cast our cares.

2. We must be at peace with God through our Saviour's work. Then, we can have the peace of God through faith in His grace. 3. We must live by God's plan. We must obey His laws and execute His plans, as far as we know them. We must also wait under the cloud.

4. We must also feed faith with promise, for this food is essential to make it thrive. And when we have done all this, we shall not find it so difficult to kneel, and cast our load, even while we pray upon our God. Then rise with lightened cheer.

Hand Over to Christ the Burden of How to Grow in Grace. This is a very great burden to some earnest people. They go from convention to convention, from one speaker to another, notebook in hand. They are eager to get the "blessing," as they call it. They often care more for the gift than for the Giver. They hear of others' unknown experiences. So, they feel disappointed and self-reproachful.

Equally, a child in kindergarten might fret because he is not entered in the higher classes of the school. But why should he worry about his future progress? His one business is to acquire the lessons set to him by his teacher. Once those are learned, it will be for the teacher to teach his pupil more. He should advance the pupil to positions where quicker progress may be made. We must learn the lessons that the Lord Jesus sets before us each day. We should let Him lead us to a deeper knowledge and love of God.

Thomas was one of the dull pupils in our Master’s school. He could not see what was clear to all beside. But instead of chiding him and leaving him in the dark, the Master paid him a visit. He made the fact of His resurrection so simple that the doubter was able to rejoice with the rest. Don't worry about being dull. It will only mean that the dear Master will give you more personal attention. Mothers give most pain to the sickly, weak, and slow among their children.

Hand Over to Christ the Burden of Maintaining a Christian Profession.

A secret fear keeps many from openly identifying with the Lord's people. They doubt they can hold out. They fear bringing disgrace to their Christian faith and sullying Christ's name. Almost unconsciously, they repeat the words of David, “ Then David said in his heart, “Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape out of his hand . ”(1 Samuel 27:1).

Anxiety about such sacred matters will hide Christ. Like vapour wreaths hide snow-capped peaks. And it is quite needless. He who saved can uphold. As is His heart of love, so is His arm of might. He is able to keep us from stumbling and present us faultless before the presence of His glory. But we shall never know the sufficiency of that keeping while we cling to the boat or even keep one hand upon its side. Only by stepping onto the water, trusting the Master's power, shall we know how surely He keeps what is entrusted to Him against that day.

We must not carry even the burden of daily abiding in Him. Let us rather trust Him to keep us trusting and abiding in Himself. He will not fail us if we do. He will reward our faith with a desire for prayer, Bible study, and communion. These are the keys to unbroken fellowship.

Hand Over to Christ the Burden of Christian Work. How to maintain our congregations? How to hold our ground amid the competition from neighboring workers? How to sustain the vigor and efficiency of our machinery? How to resolve differences among fellow and subordinate workers? How to find enough material for sermons and addresses? These burdens weigh on us. How many workers break down under them! They could bear the work but not the worry. And yet the responsibility of the work is not ours but our Master’s. He is bearing this world in His arms, as a mother her sick child. He is ministering to the infinite need of man. He is carrying on His great redemptive scheme for the glory of His Father. All He wants of us is a faithful performance of the daily tasks He gives.

Let the sailor lad sleep soundly in his hammock; the captain knows exactly the ship’s course. Let the errand boy be content to fetch and carry as bidden. The firm heads know what they are about. They have resources to meet all their needs. And let the Christian worker guard against bearing burdens that the Lord alone can carry. The Lord would never have sent us to His work without first calculating His ability to carry us through.

Hand Over to Christ the Burden of the Ebb and Flow of Feeling. Our feelings are as changeable as April weather. They are affected by countless subtle causes. These include our physical health, the atmosphere, fatigue, and lack of sleep. Also, there are spiritual and inward causes. No stringed instruments are more liable to be affected by minute changes than we are. And we are apt to take it sorely to heart when we see the tide of emotion running out fast. We should question ourselves at such times.

Is our lack of feeling due to sin or worry? If not, we can trust Him. He knows our frame and remembers we are dust. As we pass down the dark staircase, let us hold fast to the handrail of His will, willing to do His will, though in the dark. “I am as much Your own, equally devoted to You now in the depths of my soul, as when I felt happiest in Your love.”

Hand Over to Christ All Other Burdens. Servants with their frequent changes. Employers with unreasonable demands. Unkind gossip and slanderous tales about you. The perplexities and adversities of business. The difficulties of making ends meet. The question of changing your house and finding a new job. Children with childish ailments and youthful waywardness. Provision for sickness and old age. Some have businesses that cause great anxiety. Others are haunted by poverty. Any one of these will break our rest.

One barking dog may break our slumber in the stillest night. One grain of dust in the eye will ruin our enjoyment of the fairest view. There is nothing for us, then, but to roll our burden, and indeed ourselves, on God. “Cast your burden on the Lord, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved.” (Psalm 55:22).

A little boy, trying to help his father move some books, fell on the stairs under the weight of a heavy volume. The father ran to his aid. He caught up with the boy and carried them both to his room. And will our Father do less? He must love us infinitely and be ever at hand. “ Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you ” (1 Peter 5:7). It is a good way to deal with God. If you are unsure of His will, say that you will stay where you are. Or, go on doing what you have been doing.

Do this until He makes clear what He wants and empowers you to do it. Entrust your worries to God. “Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established.” (Proverbs 16:3). Expect Him to make any changes clearly known to you, so you won't mistake it, even if you're dull.

Don’t worry about dress, ornaments, or doubtful things. Satan loves to turn the soul’s attention from Christ to itself. It is as if a girl should spend an hour in her room, choosing a dress for her impatient lover, who is waiting. Let her go to him, and if she desires it, he will reveal his preferences to her directly in due time. Get into the presence of Jesus. You will not be left to hazy doubts. You will be told clearly His will, always about one point at a time.

Archbishop Leighton sweetly says: "When you must do or suffer anything, tell God." Burden Him with it. Then, you have done enough." No more care, but sweet, quiet diligence in thy duty, and dependence on Him for the carriage of thy matters. Roll over on God, make one bundle of all: roll thy cares, and thyself with them, as one burden, all on thy God."

If individuals bring no burdens into the soul and give them to the Lord, the peace of God will fill the inner temple. Though the world may be restless, these things will endure. They are the presence of God. Meanwhile, the soul keeps an unbroken Sabbath. It is like the calm ocean depths, untouched by the hurricanes that churn the surface into foam. “And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:7).

fields.title: How to Bear Sorrow
fields.body_html:
You are passing through a time of deep sorrow. The love in which you placed your trust has failed you without warning. It has dried up like a brook in the desert that is now a dwindling stream, then shallow pools, and at last drought. You are always listening for footsteps that do not come. Waiting for a word that is not spoken, pining for a reply that tarries overdue. The savings of your life have vanished without warning. Instead of helping others, someone must help you. You must leave the warm nest that sheltered you from life’s storms. You must venture alone into a hostile world. Or, you receive an unexpected call to take on another's life. You must take no rest until you have guided it through dark, difficult seas to safety.

Your health, sight, and energy are failing. You carry a death sentence. The anguish of awaiting the future is almost unbearable. In other cases, there is a sense of recent loss.

The gap in the forest shows where the woodsman has been felling trees. At such times life seems almost insupportable. Will every day be as long as this? Will the slow-moving hours ever again quicken their pace?

Will life ever array itself in another garb than the torn autumn remnants of past summer glory? “Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?” (Psalm 77:9).

This road has been trodden by myriads. Think of the wars that have devastated every land. Of the Nimrods, the Nebuchadnezzars, the Timurs, and the Napoleons. Of the merciless slave trade. And of all the tyranny, oppression, and wrongs the weak have suffered at the hands of their fellows. Of the unutterable sorrows of women and children. You must see that most of our race shares your grief.

Jesus Christ Himself trod this difficult path, leaving traces of His blood on its flints. Apostles, prophets, confessors, and martyrs have passed by the same way. It is comforting to know that others have crossed the same dark valley. The vast crowd before the Lamb, wearing victory palms, came out of great tribulation. Where they were, we are; and, by God’s grace, where they are, we will be.

Do Not Talk About Punishment. You may talk of chastisement or correction. Our Father deals with us as with sons. You may speak of reaping the results of mistakes and sins, once planted in life's furrows. Or, you may bear the consequences of others' sins and mistakes. But, do not speak of punishment.

Jesus took on all the guilt and penalty of sins, and He removed them forever. His were the stripes and the chastisement of our peace. If God punishes us for our sins, Christ's sufferings were incomplete.

If He began to punish us, life would be too short for the infliction of all that we deserve. Also, how could we explain life's anomalies? The saints endure suffering, while the ungodly live peacefully. Surely, if our sufferings were penal, there would be a reversal of lots of these.

Sorrow is a refiner’s crucible. Another's neglect or cruelty may cause it. It might be due to uncontrollable circumstances or a dark past. But, since God allowed it, we must accept it. It is His test, a furnace to search and purify the soul. Suffering searches us as fire does metal. We think we completely devote ourselves to God until the cleansing fire of pain exposes us. Then we discover, as Job did, how much dross there is in us, and how little real patience, submission, and faith. Nothing detaches us from this world, its pleasures, and earthly loves more than this. Nothing but the life of Jesus in our mortal flesh can likely stop the self-life's power.

But God always keeps the discipline of sorrow in His own hands. Our Lord said, “My Father is the husbandman.” His hand holds the pruning knife. His eye watches the crucible. His gentle touch is on the pulse while the operation is in progress. He will not allow even the devil to have his own way with us. As in the case of Job, so always. The team allocates the moments with care. The test's severity is exact. It lies in unrecognized reserves of grace and strength. They will be sought and used under the pain of great pressure.

He holds the winds in His fist and the waters in the hollow of His hand. He doesn’t dare risk the loss of that which has cost Him the blood of His Son. “ No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it . (1 Corinthians 10:13).

In sorrow, the Comforter is near. “Very present in times of trouble.” He sits by the crucible, a Refiner of silver. He regulates the heat, marking every change. He waits for the scum to float away and for the clear, molten metal to mirror his face. No earthly friend may tread the winepress with you. But, the Savior is there, His garments stained with the blood of the grapes of your sorrow. Dare to repeat it often, though you do not feel it, and though Satan insists that God has left you, “You are with me.” Mention His name again and again, “Jesus, Jesus, You are with me.” So you will become conscious that He is there.

When friends come to console you, they speak of time's healing touch. They think forgetting is the best cure for sorrow. In their kindness, they suggest travel or fun. But they fail to see the dark night that hangs over your soul. So you turn from them sick at heart and prepared to say, as Job, “Miserable comforters are you all.” But, Jesus is nearer than they are. He knows their pain. He feels for them. His love is too deep for words. He waits to comfort them, like a mother with a suffering baby.

Study the art of this divine comfort. Then, you can comfort those in any affliction with the comfort you received from God (2 Corinthians 1:4). Some trials may come to us, as they do to our Lord. They exist to help us give "sympathy to others." We should observe each symptom of the pain with attention. We should also note each prescription of the Great Physician. We may have to help those with similar experiences in the future. So, we learn from our suffering. When we are perfect, we can help tormented souls. Our help will be priceless and eternal.

Do Not Shut Yourself Up with Your Sorrow. A friend, in deep grief, wrote that he must give up the Christian ministries he had loved. I replied, urging him not to. There is no solace for heart pain like ministry. Great suffering tempts us to isolate and withdraw. We want to sit alone and be silent. Do not yield to it. Break through the icy chains of the reserve, if they have already gathered. Arise, anoint your head and wash your face; go forth to your duty, with willing though chastened steps. All selfishness, in action or thought, is hurtful. It shuts out God's help and love.

Sorrow is apt to be selfish. The soul, full of grief and refusing comfort, becomes a Dead Sea. It is a place where no birds fly and nothing grows. And thus we miss the very lesson that God would teach us. His constant war is against the self-life, and every pain He inflicts is to lessen its hold upon us. But we may thwart His purpose. We may extract poison from His gifts, as men do with opium and alcohol from innocent plants.

A Hindu woman, a beautiful Eastern legend tells us, lost her only child. Wild with grief, she implored a prophet to give back her little one to her love. He looked at her tenderly for a long while and said: “Go, my daughter, bring me a handful of rice from a house into which Death has never entered, and I will do as you desire.” The woman at once began her search. She went from dwelling to dwelling and easily got rice. But, when they granted it, she asked, "Is everyone at the hearth—father, mother, children—none missing?"

The people invariably shook their heads, with sighs and looks of sadness. As far and wide as she wandered, there was always some vacant seat by the hearth. The legend says, as she passed on, her grief faded. The sorrow everywhere had overwhelmed her. Her heart, once consumed by its own pain, now yearned to share in the world's suffering. Her anguish turned to pity; her passion to compassion. She lost herself in the interest of all. She found redemption in redeeming.

Refrain from criticizing yourself for your intense feelings. Tears are natural. Jesus wept. A rainless thunderstorm is perilous. The pattering raindrops cool the air and relieve the charged atmosphere. The swollen brooks state that the snow is melting on the hills and spring is near. “Daughters of Jerusalem,” said our Lord, “Weep for yourselves and for your children.” (Luke 23:28). To bear sorrow with dry eyes and a stolid heart may befit a Stoic, but not a Christian. We should not scold nature, longing for its mate, its lost joy, the touch of a vanished hand, the sound of a still voice. We ask only that you surrender the will. This is the one consideration for those who suffer, is the will right? If it isn’t, God Himself cannot comfort. If it is, then the path will lead from the valley of the shadow of death to the banqueting table and the overflowing cup.

Many say, “I cannot feel surrendered. It is bad enough to have my grief to bear, but I have this added trouble, that I cannot feel surrendered.” My constant reply is: “You probably never can feel surrender, but you can.

The Lord Jesus, in the Garden of Gethsemane, has shown us how to suffer. He chose His Father’s will. Satan prompted Judas to mix the cup and give it to the Savior. But the Savior looked past Judas to the Father, who allowed his cruel act. He then said, "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given me?" He then added, "If I cannot pass this unless I drink it, may your will be done." He gave up His own way, saying, "If you are willing, remove this cup from me." Still, not my will, but yours, be done.”

Let all sufferers who read these lines go apart and dare to say the same words: “Your will, and not mine. Your will be done in the earth of my life, as in the heaven of Your purpose. I choose Your will.” Say this thoughtfully and deliberately. Not because you feel it, but because you will. Not because the way of the cross is pleasant, but because it must be right. Say it, whenever the pain returns, whenever the wound bleeds. “Not my will, but Yours be done.” Dare to say yes to God.

“Even so, Father, for so it seems good in Your sight.”

And so you will be led to feel that all is right and well. A great calm will settle on your heart. It will be a peace beyond understanding. You will find a rest that coexists with suffering.

It will walk amid it, like the three young men in the fiery furnace. The burning coals must have felt like the dewy grass of a forest glade. The doctor told us my little child was dying. I felt like a stone. But in a moment, I seemed to give up my hold on her. She appeared no longer mine, but God’s.”

Be Sure to Learn God’s Lessons. Each sorrow carries at its heart a germ of holy truth. If you get and sow in your heart, you will bear fruit, as seed-corns from mummy cases do in modern soil. God has a meaning in each blow of His chisel, each incision of His knife. He knows the way that He takes. But his object is not always clear to us. In suffering, God touches the minor chords. He develops the passive virtues.

He reveals the treasures of darkness, the constellations of promise, the rainbow of hope, and the silver light of the covenant. What is character without sympathy, submission, patience, and trust? What is it without hope that grips the unseen as an anchor? But these Graces are only possible through sorrow.

Sorrow is a garden. Its trees bear the fruits of righteousness. They are peaceful. Do not leave without bringing them with you. Sorrow is a mine, its walls glistening with precious stones. Do not return to daylight without some specimens. Sorrow is a school.

You are sent to sit on its hard benches and learn from its black-lettered pages lessons that will make you wise forever; do not trifle away your chance of graduating there. Miss Havergal used to talk of “turned lessons."

Count on the afterward. God will not always be causing grief. He ploughs the dull brown acres. He wants to sow precious seed.

Believe that in days of sorrow, He is sowing light for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart. Look forward to the reaping. Expect the joy ahead. It will fill your heart with song when patience has done her perfect work.

You will live to recognize the wisdom of God’s choice for you. One day, you will see that the thing you wanted was only second best. You will be surprised to remember. You nearly broke your heart and wasted your life on something that would not have satisfied you. It was like a child chasing a butterfly or a soap bubble. You will meet your beloved again. You will have your love again. You will gain a deep character, great sympathy, and patience. You will understand and help others. If you give these to Christ, you will be glad you were afflicted. You will see God’s plan and purpose; you will reap His harvest; you will behold His face and be satisfied. Each wound will have its pearl. Each carcass will have a swarm of bees. Each foe will yield its goodly spoil, like Midian did to Gideon.

The way of the cross, rightly borne, is the only way to the everlasting light. Only the path through Gethsemane and over Calvary's hill leads to the Easter visions and the Ascension's glories. If we do not drink His cup, or are not baptized with His baptism, we cannot expect to share in the joys of His espousals and the ecstasy of His triumph. We must also fill up what is lacking in His sufferings. If we meet these conditions, we will not miss a note in the everlasting song or an element in the bliss possible to men.

Not possible to remove the adverb. The death of Hallam was the birthday of Tennyson’s beautiful poem “In Memoriam.” The cloud of insanity that brooded over Cowper gave us the hymn “God Moves in a Mysterious Way.” Milton’s blunders taught him to sing of “Holy light, offspring of heaven’s first-born.” Rist used to say, “The cross has pressed many songs out of me.” No one likely suffers without helping to ease grief, to triumph good over evil, love over hate, and light over darkness.

If you believe this, could you not bear to suffer? Isn't the worst part of suffering its loneliness? And, its aimlessness? Then dare to believe that no man dies to himself. Fall into the ground, bravely and cheerfully, to die. If you refuse, you will be alone. But if you yield, you will bear fruit. It will sweeten and strengthen the lives of others.

They may never know your name or thank you for your help.

fields.title: In the Secret of His Presence
fields.body_html:
In one sense, God is always near us. He is not an absentee; he does not need anyone to bring him down from the heavens or up from the deep. He is near at hand. His Being pervades all being. Every world that floats like an island in space shows signs of His presence. It's like how your friend's home is full of clues of his house. They prove he lives there, though you have not seen his face. Every crocus pushing through the dark mould. Every firefly in the forest. Every bird that springs up from its nest before your feet. All that exists is as full of God's presence as the burning bush. Before it, Moses bared his feet in acknowledgment of God. But we do not always realise it. We often pass hours, and days, and weeks.

We sometimes pray. We go back and forth to His house, where the ladder of communication rests. Still, He is a shadow, a name, a tradition, a dream of days gone by. “Oh that I knew where find him!

That even come to his seat! I seek him, but he's not there.

Behold, I go forward, but he is not there,and backward, but I do not perceive him; on the left hand when he is working, I do not behold him; he turns to the right hand, but I do not see him.” (Job 23:3, 8–9).

How different is this failure to see God's presence from the bliss of those who felt His nearness! Brother Lawrence, a simple cook, felt God's presence for over sixty years. He felt it while doing his humble duties.

Office as when partaking of the Holy Supper. John Howe, on the blank page of his Bible, wrote in Latin: "This morning I awoke from a most delightful dream. A bright stream of celestial rays from the Divine Majesty's throne seemed to dart into my open and expanded breast. I have often reflected on that great pledge of Divine favor. It has brought me much joy.”

Are not these, so blessed and inspiring, experiences like those of the author of the longest, and in some ways, the sublimest Psalm in the Psalter? He had been pounding out the golden ore of thought through the paragraphs of great power and beauty. Then, he seemed to sense that He of whom he had been speaking was near and bending over him.

The sense of the presence of God was born upon this inner consciousness. And, lifting up a face on which reverence and ecstasy met and mingled, he cried, “But you are near, O Lord, and all your commandments are true.” (Psalm 119:151).

If only such an experience of the nearness of God were always ours, enfolding us as air or light; if only we could feel, as the great apostle put it on Mars’ Hill, that God is not far away but the element in which we have our being, as sea flowers live in deep, still lagoons: then we should understand what David meant when he spoke about dwelling in the house of the Lord all the days of his life, beholding His beauty, inquiring in His temple, and hiding in the secret of His pavilion. “One thing have I asked of the Lord, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the Lord and to inquire in his temple.
